As a result, both raw and finished steel products from China are part of some U.S. PV installations. However, the United States maintains upstream strength through domestic iron ore production, and it has a large domestic capacity of steel manufacturing as well as high tariffs on imported steel. Much of the steel used in PV installations has a relatively low value-to-weight ratio, which favors a domestic supply with shorter shipping distances. It is easier for PV suppliers to source steel tailored to individual project specifications from domestic suppliers, plus there are incentives for PV systems that depend on the use of domestically produced steel. We estimate that more than 75% of torque tubes and driven piles are produced domestically using domestic steel. Rebar demand for PV is comparatively small, limited to pads or drilled piers, and represents well under 1% of the national rebar market, most of which is supplied domestically. However, most generic steel fasteners are imported (more than 50% from Taiwan and China) owing to their high value-to-weight ratio and the significant scale and cost advantage of foreign supply chains. Generic fasteners used for PV represent a small part of the larger fastener fabrication industry, so their market size would not justify the U.S. scale-up required to overcome a 40% price premium. As a result, U.S. fastener manufacturers focus on niche, high- specification products such as those produced specifically for trackers that are uniquely eligible for the 45X MPTC and domestic content bonus credit. Galvanized steel rails dominate utility-scale systems and are largely supported by U.S. roll- forming capacity and abundant domestic iron ore. Aluminum rails and flashing/feet are used in approximately 80% of residential and commercial rooftop PV, constituting roughly 1% of aluminum consumed domestically. The United States has limited aluminum smelting capacity and little mining of bauxite, the ore used to make aluminum. Thus, almost half of aluminum- based products are imported, while half are domestically produced from primary smelters using imported alumina and secondary smelters using domestically available scrap aluminum products. We estimate approximately 50% of aluminum mounting components used in the U.S. PV industry are made domestically. 67 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4.2 Trackers As part of a PV system, trackers move PV modules throughout the day to increase the amount of sunlight they receive and thus the amount of electricity they produce. Trackers are composed of various structural, mechanical, and electronic components—some simple in design and composition and some complex. Tracker companies specialize in developing IP and managing the logistics of getting tracker equipment to the PV installation site, where much of the tracker assembly occurs. Trackers are installed not by the tracker companies but by EPC installers, who receive training and field services from the tracker companies.
